summary: Documents a common practice of using the IGP metric as a second traffic engineering metric for constraint-based routing of MPLS TE tunnels. This lets one kind of tunnel optimize one metric and another kind optimize a different one, such as bandwidth versus delay. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Different trips want different best roads: shortest or quickest. This explains how to use the existing route costs as a second ruler.

subtitle: How routers can use the ordinary IGP link cost as a second yardstick for placing MPLS traffic engineering tunnels.

tldr.problem: The IGP extensions for MPLS traffic engineering advertise only one extra TE metric, but operators want some tunnels (such as voice) placed by delay and others (such as data) placed by something else.
tldr.mechanism: The head-end router is configured per tunnel to run its constraint-based path computation on either the TE metric or the existing IGP metric, so the two metrics act as two separate yardsticks. No protocol changes are needed.
tldr.outcome: It documents what routers and networks already did. It works for two metrics only, and only on links that have an IGP adjacency.

today: RFC 3785 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 87) from May 2004, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It documents practice at the time of writing rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: Why a Second Metric Is Wanted
sections.content:
OSPF and IS-IS were extended so that routers can advertise one additional TE metric per link, used by Constraint Based Routing when it computes paths for MPLS traffic engineering tunnels (Label Switched Paths, or LSPs).

Providers sometimes want different classes of service carried on different TE tunnels, for example to apply different fast restoration policies or to meet different QoS objectives. The most common case in the RFC is optimizing a delay-related metric (mainly propagation delay) for tunnels carrying voice, while optimizing a more usual metric, such as one reflecting link bandwidth, for tunnels carrying data.

Further IGP extensions could advertise several TE metrics. This RFC instead describes what existing implementations and deployments already do, with no extension beyond the OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone calls care about how fast the road is, and big downloads care about how wide the road is. One ruler cannot measure both, so you want two.

sections.title: The Common Practice
sections.content:
The idea is simple. Data tunnels are often meant to follow the same metric as normal shortest path routing. In that case the head-end router computes their paths with the IGP metric, and the TE metric is freed up to carry some other value, such as a delay-based metric, for the tunnels that need it.

The reverse also works. If administrators set the IGP metric to factor in link propagation delay, delay-sensitive tunnels such as voice use the IGP metric, and the TE metric can carry a bandwidth-based value for data tunnels. More generally, the TE metric can carry any arbitrary metric useful for the tunnels that need something other than the IGP metric.
sections.plainLanguage: The road signs already show one cost. The memo says to put a second cost on a different sign and let each trip pick which sign to read.

sections.title: What Routers and Operators Do
sections.content:
A head-end router implements the practice in two steps: it lets the operator configure, for each TE LSP, whether the IGP metric or the TE metric is used, and its path computation can then use either one according to that setting.

A service provider deploys it by configuring the TE metric on every relevant link to reflect the alternative metric (for example a delay-based one), and by configuring each TE LSP to be routed on either the TE metric or the IGP metric.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router gets a switch for every tunnel that says which ruler to use. The network owner sets the second ruler's numbers on every road.

sections.title: Limits of the Approach
sections.content:
The RFC lists three constraints:

  • Tunnels can be routed on one of two metrics only, not three or more.
  • The IGP metric must be appropriate as one of the two metrics. It cannot be used if IGP shortest path routing needs to be based on a third metric.
  • It only works on links that support an IGP adjacency, so that an IGP metric is actually advertised. For example, it cannot be used on Forwarding Adjacencies.

The practice also does not use the TE metric and the IGP metric at the same time for one LSP, since that is known to be an NP-complete problem.
sections.plainLanguage: You get exactly two rulers, one must be the regular one, and it only works on roads that are really on the map. Using both rulers at once for one trip is far too hard to work out.

sections.title: Interoperability
sections.content:
When the head-end router does all the path computation, as in intra-area operation, there is no interoperability issue, because choosing one metric or the other is purely local to that router.

When another component also takes part, for example Area Boundary Routers or a Path Computation Server in inter-area operation, the choice of metric must be signaled along with the other constraints (bandwidth, affinity) for the LSP. The RFC points to an example proposal for doing this with RSVP-TE.
sections.plainLanguage: If one router plans the whole trip, nobody else needs to know which ruler it used. If helpers plan parts of the trip, they must be told which ruler to read.

sections.title: Migrating to Two Metrics
sections.content:
Routers with the older behaviour always use the TE metric for all tunnels. If the TE metric is reconfigured to a delay-based value before every head-end is upgraded, all tunnels would be routed on it, not only the intended ones. Some migrations therefore need all head-ends upgraded first.

The RFC gives this sequence:

  1. Upgrade software on all head-end routers to support the practice.
  2. Change the TE LSP configuration to use the IGP metric instead of the TE metric.
  3. Configure the TE metric on the links to reflect the second metric.
  4. Change the configuration of the LSPs that need the second metric, and create new ones if needed.

Step 2 should not disrupt traffic, as long as the IGP and TE metrics are equal on every link at that moment.
sections.plainLanguage: First give every router the new switch, then flip all trips to the regular ruler, then change the second ruler's numbers, and only then move the trips that need it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The practice raises no specific security issues beyond those of existing traffic engineering. The RFC refers readers to the security sections of the traffic engineering requirements RFC and of the RSVP-TE and CR-LDP specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Using the second ruler does not make the roads any less safe than before.
